 Bobby Brink Has Finally Found A Home On the Wild's Third Line
 Bobby Brink Has Finally Found A Home On the Wild's Third Line 
 Image courtesy of Matt Marton-Imagn Images
 By 
 Chris Schad 
 - October 19 
 In the first five years of his NHL career,  Bobby Brink  has searched for a home. The Philadelphia Flyers selected him with the second pick of the 2019 draft, but he never seemed to fit. When the Minnesota Wild acquired him ahead of last year’s trade deadline, he still didn’t have a permanent role, as a shoulder injury and a stable of veterans in front of him kept him in the press box during their march to the playoffs. 
 That reputation is why the Wild asked Brink to meet them halfway last offseason, agreeing to a one-year deal well below what he could have received as a restricted free agent. But early in his first full season in Minnesota, Brink appears to have finally found a home and has become a perfect fit on the third line. 
 Brink has always been talented. The Flyers selected the Minnetonka native with the 34th overall pick in 2019, and he debuted in 2021-22 after wrapping up his collegiate career at the University of Denver. He peaked in 2024-25, scoring 12 goals and recording 41 points in 79 games. Still, he couldn’t get regular playing time in Philadelphia. 
 Part of the problem was a surplus of young wing talent. Matvei Michkov , Tyson Foerster , Travis Konecny ,  and  Owen Tippett  took the top roles in the Philadelphia lineup, leading general manager  Daniel Briere  to look for ways to upgrade the roster, mainly with  a right-handed defenseman. 
 The final part of the equation was Brink’s relationship with John Tortorella. Brink had speed and offensive playmaking. But Tortorella, likely sensing Brink’s NHL role, focused on his defensive play.  
 “We were hard on him,” Tortorella told  Joe Smith of The Athletic last March. “We pushed him, and there were hiccups along the way. He’s turned into a guy. I wish other people would watch how he’s developed. He didn’t take anything personally. He tried to get better every day. And he became one of my best players [from his time coaching the Flyers]. He did everything for us. That’s what I love about Bobby.” 
 People vilified Tortorella when he didn't play Brink during his first trip to St. Paul as a professional in 2024. However, Brink also believes “tough love” made him a better player. 
 “Torts taught me that if you’re not going to be able to show up every night that it doesn’t matter [whether] we’re in Minnesota, Montreal or back home in Philly. You’re not going to be in the lineup,” Brink said during an interview on the Wild on 7th  podcast  last week. “There was a standard that had to be kept, and if I wasn’t playing up to that standard, I wasn’t playing no matter where we were. 
 “...The thing about Torts is, a lot of it was predictable. You didn’t need to score. If you were getting pucks out, if you were blocking shots, if you were doing the little things that helped the team win, he was good at seeing…if you were in a slump. He was still putting you out there because you were doing a lot of things to help the team win.” 
 However, his lack of playing time eventually led to his departure. The Wild sent David Jiricek  to Philadelphia in March’s trade. But  after spending his initial weeks behind  Marcus Johansson  and  Vladimir Tarasenko  while nursing a shoulder injury, Brink has  taken those lessons to heart in the Wild’s bottom six. 
 Brink’s ability to score and set up teammates will always draw attention. But other aspects of his game have helped him, too. His passing  has helped him log four assists in the Wild’s injury-plagued lineup and complements his regular linemates,  Ryan Hartman  and  Yakov Trenin , who play more downhill . 
 Every team wants a player with his motor in the bottom six. Brink uses his speed to win board battles and draw penalties. The final piece is his defense, which has recorded six takeaways, five blocked shots, and five hits in the Wild’s first eight games. 
 That may cap Brink’s offensive upside. But if he can score 10-15 goals a year, the Wild will gladly take it because of the other ways he can affect the team.  
 For a player who has struggled to find a permanent role in the NHL, this is a welcome development. And for someone looking to prove he deserves a bigger commitment from the Wild, he could play his way into their long-term plans. That’s a big win for both sides, and it shows Brink he belongs. 
 By 
 Chris Schad
